sources.citation: Baums, Stefan. 2009. A Gāndhārī Commentary on Early Buddhist Verses: British Library Kharoṣṭhī Fragments 7, 9, 13 and 18. PhD dissertation, University of Washington. xxxiv+709 pp. (Ch. 4 'Orthography and Phonology', pp. 110–199; Ch. 5 Morphology, pp. 201–239)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Nothing on the position of word stress. The 90-page phonology chapter has no accent/prosody subsection; a full-text search for stress/accent/stress/prosod yields only §4.2.1.4 'two moras of prosodic weight' (p. 121), §4.2.1.6 reduction of final vowels (pp. 125–128, discussing Fussman 1989 without invoking stress) and §4.3.3 (p. 191) 'Seven Old Indo-Aryan enclitic (unaccented) words have descendants in our text'.

sources.note: Sound inventory and OIA>Gāndhārī sound changes (monophthongization, vocalization of r̥, Law of Two Moras, consonant weakening); no word-stress statement. The only 'accent' hit is the recommendation to transliterate the postconsonantal-v diacritic 'as a circumflex accent'.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Gandhari language' (accessed 2026-09-17), citing Salomon, Allchin & Barnard 1999: 110 and Masica 1993 for phonology
sources.note: Phonology paragraph (three sibilants preserved, cluster retention, intervocalic weakening); no mention of stress or accent.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)

sources.citation: Burrow, T. 1937. The Language of the Kharoṣṭhi Documents from Chinese Turkestan. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. (Niya Prakrit; Phonology §§1–33)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress rule. Incidental: 'As unaccented forms their initial would be liable to be treated as intervocalic t, i.e. become voiced' (p. 6, pronominal forms); s in unaccented particles treated as intervocalic (p. 9); se 'voiced owing to its being unaccented' (§80); 'the liability of k to be dropped in certain positions of weak stress cf. §16'; samaho 'weakly stressed' (p. 43).

sources.note: The fullest phonological interpretation of Gāndhārī spelling as a spoken language; proposes merger of all final vowels to short [ə] and a three-way syllable typology (Baums 2009: 125–127), the material from which a stress rule, if anyone has stated one for Gāndhārī, would come.
